deep.reconstruction:
Context: Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. 10, §§323-332. Let N = 2p+1 be prime. Following §319, suppose a is a number whose least power congruent to 1 mod N is a^p. Then H = {1, a, ..., a^{p-1}} gives p distinct residues, the 'residues of the geometric progression'. The p remaining classes are the 'non-residues' A, Aa, ..., Aa^{p-1}, i.e. the coset A·H. The page proves that H coincides with the quadratic residues, and then derives that -1 is a quadratic residue when p is even.

§323-324: two non-residues products are residues.
- Any second non-residue can be written A a^n, so the product of two non-residues is A^2 a^n.
- Suppose this product were a non-residue. Then A^2 a^n ≡ A a^m for some m; replacing m by m+νp, we may take m > n.
- Since N divides neither A nor a^n, cancel A a^n: a^{m-n} ≡ A (mod N).
- That puts A in H, a contradiction. Hence non-residue × non-residue lies in H. Together with §320 (residue×residue ∈ H, residue×non-residue ∉ H), this is the index-2 structure of H in (Z/N)^*.

§325: restatement. If a has order exactly p, every product of two non-residues of H lies in H.

§326: H equals the set of quadratic residues.
- For any x in 1..2p, x² ∈ H: if x ∈ H this is clear; if x ∉ H it follows from §324.
- So the squares lie in H.
- [mine] Both sets have exactly p elements (the count of quadratic residues was proved earlier in the chapter), so they are equal. Euler says simply that the two orders 'plane inter se congruere'.

§327: consequently the quadratic non-residues are exactly the coset A·H.

§328.
- Recalled: if a is a quadratic residue, then a^p ≡ 1 (a = x² gives a^p = x^{2p} ≡ 1 by Fermat).
- New: if a is a quadratic non-residue, then a cannot have order exactly p, since otherwise by §326 a ∈ H would be a residue.
- So either a^p ≢ 1, or a has a smaller order p/ν.

§329: converse of Euler's criterion. If a^p ≡ 1 then a is a quadratic residue.
- If p is the least such exponent, this follows from §326.
- If the order is smaller, Euler says it is 'even more true' ('eo magis verum esse videtur'). If a^{p/2} ≡ 1 is minimal, a is even a biquadratic (4th-power) residue; if a^{p/3} is minimal, a is a 6th-power residue; and so on. Hence a is always a quadratic residue.

§330. Contrapositive: if a is a non-residue, then N does not divide a^p − 1.
- Take a = d − α with d = N and α a quadratic residue.
- Then (d−α)^p − 1 is not divisible by N, while α^p − 1 is.
- So (d−α)^p − α^p is not divisible by N.

§331.
- If p is even, (d−α)^p ≡ (−α)^p = α^p, so that difference IS divisible.
- Hence when p is even, the complement d − α of a residue cannot be a non-residue.

§332.
- For p even, the complement of every residue is a residue, because (d−α)^p ≡ α^p ≡ 1.
- This leads (next page) to: −1 is a quadratic residue mod a prime 4q+1.
errors: §326: the conclusion that squares and H 'coincide' needs |squares| = |H| = p. This is not restated here, though it was established earlier in the chapter, so the step is implicit but legitimate.

§325 onward presupposes an element a of order exactly p = (N−1)/2. Its existence is not proved; it follows from the existence of a primitive root g (take a = g²), which Euler had not rigorously established.

§329 is heuristic for elements whose order is a proper divisor of p ('eo magis verum esse videtur'). The claim that an element of order dividing p/ν is a 2ν-th power residue is true, but it relies tacitly on the cyclicity of (Z/N)^*, which is not proved.

This gap matters for §§330-332: the application in §331-332 needs the contrapositive of §329 for elements like −α, whose order may be much smaller than p (e.g. −1 has order 2). The rigorous route is the marginal §321 on the previous page, or Lagrange's bound that x^p ≡ 1 has at most p roots mod N.
No arithmetic slips: a^{m−n} ≡ A and (d−α)^p ≡ α^p for even p are correct.

results.what: Product of two quadratic non-residues mod a prime is a residue (index-2 subgroup / coset argument)
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol; quadratic residues form an index-2 subgroup
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa residua, E262, c.1755-1761); Legendre symbol notation 1798

results.what: The quadratic residues mod 2p+1 coincide with the powers of any element of order p
results.modern_name: Quadratic residues = subgroup of squares = unique subgroup of index 2 in the cyclic group (Z/N)^*
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (residue-theory papers 1750s-1770s); cyclic structure via primitive roots Gauss 1801

results.what: a^p ≡ 1 mod 2p+1 iff a is a quadratic residue
Elements of order dividing p/ν are 2ν-th power residues
results.modern_name: In a cyclic group of order n, {x : x^{n/k} = 1} = k-th powers (power residue criterion)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (power residues), rigorous via primitive roots Gauss 1801

results.what: If p = (N−1)/2 is even, the complement of every residue is a residue; hence −1 is a QR mod primes 4q+1

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known treatment of quadratic residues and Euler's criterion from the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (published 1849 in Opera postuma). Everything is standard and attributed to Euler. The only noteworthy feature is the openly heuristic §329 and the tacit reliance on an element of order p.

checkable.sympy: set(pow(x,2,13) for x in range(1,13)) == set(pow(4,k,13) for k in range(6))
checkable.asserts: For N=13 (p=6), the squares coincide with the powers of 4, an element of order exactly 6.

checkable.sympy: all(((pow(a,(P-1)//2,P)==1) == is_quad_residue(a,P)) for P in primerange(3,200) for a in range(1,P))
checkable.asserts: Euler's criterion: a^p ≡ 1 mod 2p+1 iff a is a quadratic residue.

checkable.sympy: all(is_quad_residue((a*b)%P,P) for P in primerange(3,100) for a in range(1,P) for b in range(1,P) if not is_quad_residue(a,P) and not is_quad_residue(b,P))
checkable.asserts: The product of two quadratic non-residues is a residue (§324).
−1 is a QR exactly when p = (P−1)/2 is even (§§331-333).

checkable.sympy: set(a for a in range(1,13) if pow(a,3,13)==1) == set(pow(x,4,13) for x in range(1,13))
checkable.asserts: §329 for N=13: elements with a^{p/2} ≡ 1 are exactly the biquadratic residues.

checkable.sympy: all((pow((P-al)%P,(P-1)//2,P) - pow(al,(P-1)//2,P)) % P == 0 for P in primerange(5,200) if P%4==1 for al in range(1,P))
checkable.asserts: For p even, (d−α)^p ≡ α^p mod d (§331).
